observability.request_last_user_preview: For the initial phase, each of the six proposed sites will log hourly air-temperature, wind speed/direction, barometric pressure, and cumulative rainfall, recorded in a bound logbo

outcome.text_head:
The user is my "partner" in an engineering test of an AI conversation interface. We're developing a practical plan for an imaginary neighborhood weather-observation project. They've laid out initial-phase details about:

- Six sites logging hourly temperature, wind, pressure, rainfall
- Bound logbook with timestamp, observer initials, sky-condition code, instrument serial
- Temperature probe cross-checked against NIST-traceable reference (±0.2 °C)
- Stevenson screen mounted ≥1.5 m from vertical surfaces, 360° open-sky view verified by horizon sketch
- Saturday comparison against nearest NOAA/NCDC station
- Residual offset beyond ±0.5 °C triggers recalibration

They've addressed: instrument calibration, site selection (partial), sampling (hourly), record keeping (logbook), comparisons (NOAA/NCDC), uncertainty (±0.5 °C combined).

What they haven't fully addressed yet:
- Missing data policy
- Reporting structure
- Wind speed/direction specifics
- Barometric pressure specifics
- Rainfall measurement specifics
- Site selection criteria beyond the Stevenson screen placement
- How observers rotate
- What happens when an observer misses a shift
- Data gap thresholds

I need to:
1. Respond to my partner (acknowledge/engage their choices)
2. Advance a concrete design choice (pick something they haven't nailed down)
3. Examine a possible failure with an example
4. Keep it to three or four concise sentences
5. Don't use tools

I adopt your 1.5 m Stevenson standoff, the horizon-sketch verification, and the ±0.5 °C recalibration trigger verbatim; they close the two most probable temperature-integrity holes. For the missing-data gap you haven't yet named, a missed hour is logged "MISSING" (never interpolated) and three consecutive gaps trigger a formal site-replacement review; each station must also sit ≥50 m from a paved roadway so exhaust heat and tire aerosol cannot bias the barometer or truncate anemometer readings. The concrete failure this guards against: placing the cup anemometer on the south face of a two-storey roof embeds it in a chimney wake that at 2 m s⁻¹ true speed—a neighbourhood-gust regime—under-reads by 20–30 %, so the mast must clear every obstruction by at least twice its height in all azimuths, verified with the same horizon-sketch you specified. The weekly public report will therefore carry a per-site data-completeness percentage, and any site below 62 % completeness (≈90 % of available hours) is flagged "provisional" in the bulletin rather than silently smoothed into the trend.
